{{Short description|Sequence of numbers consisting of 1 and -1}}
{{about|sign sequences in mathematics|sequences of roadside signs|Burma-Shave}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''sign sequence''', or '''±1&ndash;sequence''' or '''bipolar sequence''', is a [[sequence]] of numbers, each of which is either 1 or −1. One example is the sequence (1, −1, 1, −1, ...).

Such sequences are commonly studied in [[discrepancy theory]].

==Erdős discrepancy problem==
<!--{{Further|[[Erdős discrepancy problem]]}}-->

Around 1932, mathematician [[Paul Erdős]] [[conjecture]]d that for any infinite ±1-sequence <math>(x_1, x_2, \ldots)</math> and any [[integer]] ''C'', there exist integers ''k'' and ''d'' such that

: <math>\left| \sum_{i=1}^k x_{i\cdot d} \right| > C.</math>

The Erdős discrepancy problem asks for a [[mathematical proof|proof]] or disproof of this conjecture.

In February 2014, Alexei Lisitsa and Boris Konev of the [[University of Liverpool]] showed that every sequence of 1161 or more elements satisfies the conjecture in the special case ''C''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, which proves the conjecture for ''C''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;2.<ref>{{cite conference | last1 = Konev | first1 = Boris | last2 = Lisitsa | first2 = Alexei | editor1-last = Sinz | editor1-first = Carsten | editor2-last = Egly | editor2-first = Uwe | arxiv = 1402.2184 | contribution = A SAT attack on the Erdős discrepancy conjecture | doi = 10.1007/978-3-319-09284-3_17 | pages = 219–226 | publisher = Springer | series = Lecture Notes in Computer Science | title = Theory and Applications of Satisfiability Testing – SAT 2014 – 17th International Conference, Held as Part of the Vienna Summer of Logic, VSL 2014, Vienna, Austria, July 14–17, 2014, Proceedings | volume = 8561 | year = 2014 | isbn = 978-3-319-09283-6 }}</ref> This was the best such bound available at the time. Their proof relied on a [[SAT-solver]] computer algorithm whose output takes up 13 [[gigabytes]] of data, more than the entire text of Wikipedia at that time, so it cannot be independently verified by human mathematicians without further use of a computer.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn25068-wikipediasize-maths-proof-too-big-for-humans-to-check.html|title=Wikipedia-size maths proof too big for humans to check|first = Jacob | last = Aron|magazine=[[New Scientist]]|date=February 17, 2014|accessdate=February 18, 2014}}</ref>

In September 2015, [[Terence Tao]] announced a proof of the conjecture, building on work done in 2010 during [[Polymath Project|Polymath5]] (a form of [[crowdsourcing]] applied to mathematics) and a suggestion made by German mathematician Uwe Stroinski on Tao's blog.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/2015/09/28/newser-famous-math-problem-solved-crowdsourcing/72973338/|title=Famous math problem solved thanks to crowdsourcing|website=[[USA Today]]|date=September 28, 2015}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|first=Jacob|last=Aron|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg22830415-200-crowds-beat-computers-in-answer-to-wikipedia-sized-maths-problem/|title=Crowds beat computers in answer to Wikipedia-sized maths problem|website=[[New Scientist]]|date=30 September 2015|access-date=October 21, 2015}}</ref> His proof was published in 2016, as the first paper in the new journal ''[[Discrete Analysis]]''.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The Erdős discrepancy problem|first=Terence|last=Tao|authorlink=Terence Tao|year=2016|arxiv=1509.05363|doi=10.19086/da.609|journal=[[Discrete Analysis]]|pages=1–29|mr=3533300|s2cid=59361755 |issn=2397-3129}}</ref>

Erdős discrepancy of finite sequences has been proposed as a measure of local randomness in [[DNA]] sequences.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Li|first1=Wentian|last2=Thanos|first2=Dimitrios|last3=Provata|first3=Astero|date=2019-01-14|title=Quantifying local randomness in human DNA and RNA sequences using Erdös motifs|journal=Journal of Theoretical Biology|volume=461|pages=41–50|doi=10.1016/j.jtbi.2018.09.031|pmid=30336158|issn=0022-5193|arxiv=1805.10248|bibcode=2019JThBi.461...41L |s2cid=52901027 }}</ref> This is based on the fact that in the case of finite-length sequences discrepancy is bounded, and therefore one can determine the finite sequences with discrepancy less than a certain value. Those sequences will also be those that "avoid" certain periodicities. By comparing the expected versus observed distribution in the DNA or using other correlation measures, one can make conclusions related to the local behavior of DNA sequences.

==Barker codes==
{{main|Barker code}}

A '''Barker code''' is a sequence of ''N'' values of +1 and &minus;1,
:<math>x_j \text{ for } j=1,\ldots,N,</math>
such that
:<math>\left|\sum_{j=1}^{N-v} x_j x_{j+v}\right| \le 1</math>
for all <math>1 \le v < N</math>.<ref>{{cite book |author=Barker, R. H. |chapter=Group Synchronizing of Binary Digital Sequences |title=Communication Theory |place=London |publisher=Butterworth |pages=273–287 |year=1953}}</ref>

Barker codes of lengths 11 and 13 are used in [[direct-sequence spread spectrum]]  and [[pulse compression|pulse compression radar]] systems because of their low [[autocorrelation]] properties.
